text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The Danish model towards unemployed youths will be introduced in Sweden from 1998 when 200,000 people will be offered either jobs or the chance of further education. People who say no to these opportunities will lose their unemployment benefits under this new system being drawn up by the Labour Market Board and Social Security Committee.
- Sweden's chemical industry reached an 11 month agreement with 25,000 workers from 800 companies on Wednesday which will lift wages by 2.30 crowns an hour or 2.67 percent.

- Forestry group SCA is selling part of its stake in investment company Industrivarden for a capital gain of 350 million crowns. It is selling 6.5 percent of its capital holding in Industrivarden and nine percent of voting rights, partly to overseas investors.

- The Swedish government wants to make it impossible for municipalities and regional authorities to use the extra billions of crowns to be allocated from the supplementary budget, released on Tuesday, to lower taxes. The government wants to ensure the money is used on health care, education and creating new jobs. The budget has proposed giving municipalities and regional authorities an extra four billion crowns in 1997, eight billion in 1998 and eight billion in 1999.

- Forestry group SCA is reducing its holding in investment group Industrivarden due to the criticism of cross ownership between the two companies. SCA is reducing its holding of voting rights to about five percent from 14 percent.

- Higher taxes on tobacco from August 1, as outlined in Tuesday's supplementary budget, will put pressure on Swedish Match's sales. Its sales could fall by 10 percent but it is possible it might take the chance to boost its margins by raising its cigarette prices by more than the new tax of seven crowns a packet.

- Lock maker Assa Abloy's shares rose nearly 13 percent on Wednesday after it announced it was buying France's largest lock making group, Vachette, for 1.1 billion francs or around 1.4 billion crowns. The buy should lift Assa Abloy's annual sales to seven billion crowns from 5.6 billion crowns.

- Swedish lock group Assa Abloy is to acquire the French lock group Vachette for 1.1 billion francs. The company's president Carl-Henric Svanberg said this was a unique opportunity to gain a dominant position in French and Belgian markets. The purchase will be financed with borrowed funds and a 640 million crown issue of new shares to shareholders.

- Ice hockey team Djurgarden wants to be Sweden's first athletics club to list its team on the stock exchange. A group of athletic clubs in Sweden have submitted a motion to the Sports Federation to change the bylaws that say a club has to be non-profitable to compete in a Federation league.

- Pulp and paper giant SCA is to reduce its shareholding in investment group Industrivarden to six percent from 14 percent. A Dutch subsidiary of SCA will issue a five-year mark Eurobond convertible into shares in Industrivarden. During the terms of the bond, SCA will surrender all voting rights to the shares. Another block will be transferred from SCA to employees' pension fund in exchange for forest land. SCA and Industrivarden have long held each other's stock and shared board members.

- Medical Invest, a Swedish medical technology company listed on the Stockholm bourse's O-list, is poised to launch its Mobimed monitoring and information systems in markets outside Sweden. Mobimed transmits medical data from a portable device to stationary equipment at medical centres. Company president Akbar Seddigh estimates potential sales in Sweden at half of the country's 700 ambulances and 150 hospitals but Germany offers potential 5,000 sales.
